title: Wilberforce (1807)
hookLine: a Christian member of Parliament campaigns year after year until Britain bans the slave trade
carry: you cannot say you did not know

lines: THE SAME EVIDENCE IN HIS HANDS.
cards: A vote is counted in the House of Commons, and the motion fails. The man who brought it goes home, and next session he brings it again. It fails again.
Year after year, a motion to end the British slave trade is voted down or stalled. Ships keep sailing. And he keeps standing up in that chamber with the same evidence in his hands.

teach.h: A CONVERSION, AND A CHOICE TO STAY.
teach.b: William Wilberforce was a young member of Parliament, clever and well liked, when he went through an evangelical conversion. For a while he wondered whether a serious Christian should leave politics altogether.
The usual account is that John Newton, the former slave-ship captain of Amazing Grace, urged him to stay where he was and use it. He stayed.

teach.h: ONE VOICE IN A WIDE CAMPAIGN.
teach.b: He joined a campaign that was already moving: Quakers, the researcher Thomas Clarkson gathering evidence from sailors and ships, formerly enslaved writers like Equiano telling what they had lived.
Wilberforce was its voice in Parliament. The campaign's great weapon was knowledge. A diagram of a slave ship, packed with bodies, was printed and passed around.
Some ordinary people stopped buying slave-grown sugar.
The argument was simple: now that you've seen it, you can't hide behind not knowing.
A line often credited to Wilberforce, though its source is uncertain, puts it this way: you may look the other way, but you cannot say you did not know.
The book of Proverbs had already asked: "If thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it?"
And Paul's words fit the long fight: "let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not."

teach.h: THE TRADE BANNED, NOT YET SLAVERY.
teach.b: In the end Parliament banned the trade. Not slavery itself, yet: that took another long campaign. But the ships were stopped by law.
Some Christians had defended the trade, and some profited from it. Others, like Wilberforce, fought it from their faith. The story holds both.

how: Christians remember Wilberforce alongside Clarkson, Equiano and others in the campaign against the slave trade, and the Church of England keeps a commemoration of him in its calendar.

games.q: you're a young member of Parliament, newly converted. you wonder if a serious Christian should leave politics. what do you do?
o: leave politics for a quiet life of prayer.
stay, and use your seat for the campaign against the slave trade.
stay, but keep your faith out of your work.
games.why: the usual account is that John Newton urged him to stay. he did, and became the campaign's voice in Parliament.

practice: Name one good thing you're working for that is taking much longer than you hoped: a cause, a family repair, a habit, a hard conversation. Don't decide anything big; just choose the next small step, the next bill you'll bring again.
If you pray, ask for strength not to grow weary; if you don't, simply hold the step.
